content: The implementation of case-finding and linkage to care strategies has proven to be highly effective, particularly among populations that are traditionally difficult to reach. Lay and self-testing methods have been widely accepted, especially by key populations such as young men who have sex with men. However, challenges persist, including the difficulty in reaching young female sex workers and the limited availability of hepatitis C virus (HCV) diagnosis and treatment services. Insights from a pilot study contributed to the revision of Vietnam's national guidelines on HIV testing and community-based HIV testing, which were officially approved by the Ministry of Health in 2018. Lay counselors in Mozambique have played a pivotal role in providing HIV counseling and testing (HIV CT) services. These counselors, often local to the communities they serve, have been instrumental in reaching underserved, remote, and impoverished areas. Since 2009, with support from Jhpiego and various community and faith-based organizations, these counselors have tested over 2 million individuals across nine provinces. To address the geographical scope of their work, counselors developed innovative mapping and coding techniques to identify and track households. This process involves creating hand-drawn maps with symbols representing each household, indicating the number of residents and their testing status. Households are color-coded based on their HIV CT coverage: green for full coverage, yellow for partial coverage, red for refusal, and blank for unoccupied homes. Additional codes denote HIV status, including discordance among couples, antiretroviral therapy (ART) usage, and tuberculosis (TB) status, reflecting the HIV/TB association. These maps are updated during subsequent visits to ensure accurate tracking and follow-up. The mapping tools provide a comprehensive view of household distribution and HIV status, enabling counselors to identify areas requiring further attention. This approach has significantly increased HIV CT coverage in rural Mozambique, with rates rising from 70% to 90% following the introduction of mapping and coding. The simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and replicability of these tools make them a best practice for expanding community access to HIV CT in low-resource settings. In 2018, PATH initiated a project to design next-generation HIV self-tests that align better with user needs and are more cost-effective to produce. To inform product design, PATH conducted user research to develop and validate personas for three key populations: female sex workers in Vietnam, adult males, and adolescent females in South Africa. Personas, a user-centered design tool, capture the characteristics, behaviors, and goals of specific user groups, facilitating cognitive empathy and informed design decisions. A mixed-methods approach was employed to create these personas, starting with expert interviews and literature reviews on care-seeking behaviors and HIV testing engagement. Draft personas were validated through semi-structured interviews with 40 female sex workers in Vietnam, 28 adolescent females, and 35 adult males in South Africa. The analysis of these interviews shaped the personas' design and content, which included demographic data, care-seeking behaviors, sexual behaviors, HIV testing experiences, and preferences for facility-based versus self-testing. The personas informed refinements to product design, such as discrete packaging to protect privacy and quality certification to build trust in test results. Digital technologies were identified as promising tools for disseminating HIV information, training on test usage, and linking users to care and counseling. These personas are now being used alongside novel self-test designs to engage manufacturers in developing next-generation tools. In India, the National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) conducted a retrospective analysis of program data from over 20,000 testing facilities to optimize testing strategies. Districts were categorized based on testing coverage and positivity rates, identifying areas for targeted interventions. Testing was increased across all district categories, with over 60% of districts showing improvements. Priority was given to districts with high positivity but low coverage, as well as those with low positivity and low coverage, to maximize the impact of testing scale-up efforts. This data-driven approach highlighted the need for customized testing strategies to address regional disparities in HIV positivity and coverage. The program is now focused on building capacity in priority districts to implement effective testing strategies tailored to local needs. This targeted approach ensures efficient utilization of resources and enhances the overall effectiveness of HIV prevention and care efforts.
